title: Reaching Points
statement: You begin at the point `(sx, sy)`. A single move takes the current point `(x, y)` to either `(x + y, y)` or `(x, x + y)`, so one coordinate grows by the value of the other. Return `true` when some sequence of zero or more moves ends exactly at `(tx, ty)`, and `false` when no sequence does.
signature: boolean reachingPoints(int sx, int sy, int tx, int ty)
notes:
## Intuition

Going forward, every point has two successors, so the search tree explodes. Going backward, every point has at most one predecessor: both coordinates are always positive, so the last move must have added the smaller coordinate to the larger one. The predecessor of `(tx, ty)` with `tx > ty` is `(tx - ty, ty)`, and a point with `tx === ty` has none. Undoing moves one at a time is correct but can take about `10^9` steps; subtracting `ty` from `tx` until `tx` is no longer the larger is just `tx % ty`, the same shortcut as Euclid's algorithm.

## Approach

1. While both target coordinates are still above the start and differ, replace the larger one by its remainder modulo the smaller.
2. If the target now equals the start, it is reachable.
3. If only `tx` matches `sx`, the remaining moves must all have added `tx` to `y`, so `ty - sy` must be a positive multiple of `tx`.
4. Symmetrically, if only `ty` matches `sy`, check that `tx - sx` is a positive multiple of `ty`.
5. Otherwise a coordinate fell below the start (or the two became equal), so the start is not on the path.

## Example 1, step by step

`(sx, sy) = (1, 1)`, `(tx, ty) = (3, 5)`. Both exceed the start and differ, and `ty` is larger, so `ty = 5 % 3 = 2`. Now `tx = 3` is larger, so `tx = 3 % 2 = 1`. The loop stops because `tx` equals `sx`. The target `(1, 2)` is not the start, but `tx === sx` and `(2 - 1) % 1 === 0`, so the answer is `true`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(log(max(tx, ty))): each remainder step at least halves the larger coordinate, as in Euclid's algorithm.
- Space: O(1).

## Pitfalls

- Plain repeated subtraction times out on inputs like `(1, 1, 10^9, 1)`.
- Taking the remainder blindly can jump past the start: when one coordinate already equals its start value, switch to the divisibility check instead of reducing further.
- `tx === ty` has no predecessor; only the start itself can be such a point.
- A remainder of `0` means a coordinate would hit zero, which is never reachable.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `sx`, `sy` | the starting point |
| `tx`, `ty` | the target, shrunk backward toward the start |
| `tx % ty`, `ty % tx` | many identical backward moves undone at once |

narration.2: Keep undoing moves while both coordinates are above the start and the point has a predecessor.
narration.3: The larger coordinate is the one the last moves increased.
narration.4: Undo every consecutive move that added ty to x in one step with a remainder.
narration.6: Otherwise y is larger, so undo all the moves that added tx to y.
narration.9: The backward walk landed exactly on the start.
narration.12: x already matches the start, so the remaining moves only added x to y.
narration.13: That works exactly when ty sits a positive multiple of tx above sy.
narration.15: The mirror case: y matches, so the remaining moves only added y to x.
narration.16: That works exactly when tx sits a positive multiple of ty above sx.
narration.18: A coordinate fell below its start value, or the point had no predecessor, so the start is unreachable.
